name: Murdaigean
summary: The dark wood of the proving fields around Dun Murdaigean, where the Fianna once ran their young, for soldiers of 25 to 29.

facts.text: Caílte setting the pace of the Fianna's run through Murdaigean is Living Server writing; the run itself, with the braided hair that must not be disturbed and the stick that must not crack, is the Fianna's test as Keating's history gives it.
Murdaigean is the battleground for levels 25 to 29 (region 251); level is the only limit in Offline DAoC.
Its central keep is Dun Murdaigean; an Albion, a Midgard and a Hibernia portal keep stand at the same three places as in the other battlegrounds.
Dun Murdaigean starts neutral in the release world.
Thidranki, Murdaigean and Caledonia were the classic battlegrounds; Abermenai came with patch 1.62 (June 2003).

Its monsters are spiders, large bloated spiders, death spiders, corpse crawlers, ire wolves and rage wolves (the Angered faction), water badgers, and goblin crawlers and watchers of the Black Mountains Goblins faction (levels 13-29).

facts.text: Keating's history gives the Fianna's tests: the candidate runs a wood with braided hair and a tree's start, and fails if caught, if a braid is loosed by a branch or a dry stick cracks underfoot; he must leap a branch at his brow, stoop under one at his knee and draw a thorn from his foot without slowing.
Irish daingean means a fortress and mur (from Latin murus) a wall or rampart, so the name reads as "wall fortress"; this reading is Living Server's, not Mythic's.
The run through Murdaigean, the knotted cords, the fortress named twice, the goblins the wardens drove west, the wolf wood and Cobthach's account are Living Server lore.

Keating's history gives the Fianna's other conditions: the twelve books of poetry; the candidate in a field of sedge with a shield and a hazel stake while nine warriors cast javelins at him from nine ridges away; steady hands; the four articles (a wife chosen without a portion, no violence to a woman, no refusal to any who ask of what he has, never flee from nine men of another nation); and his kin's pledge not to avenge his death.
Cobthach's count of the cords and the Midgard band who tracked the wounded rage wolf are Living Server lore.

story:
Murdaigean is a wood, and the light in it comes down green and goes out early.

Hibernia's filidh say it is the oldest proving ground there is, older than the fields: the wood where the Fianna tried their young before ever there was a realm war. A candidate ran it with braided hair and a tree's length of start while the company came after him, and he failed if they caught him, if a braid caught on a branch, or if a dry stick cracked under his foot. Wherever a runner was caught the Fianna knotted a cord to the nearest tree to mark the place, and the dun at the heart of the wood was where the run ended. Its name, the filidh say, says fortress twice in the old tongue. They say too that Caílte mac Rónáin set the pace for the chase, because no man of the Fianna could outrun him, and that a youth who reached the dun with every braid in place and the wood silent behind him had beaten the fastest man in Ireland.

The run was the last of the tests, not the first. Before a youth was let into the wood he had to know the twelve books of poetry and make verse of his own. He stood in a field of sedge with a shield and a hazel stake while nine of the Fianna cast their spears at him together from nine ridges off, and if one of them touched him he went home. His hands had to stay steady on a weapon. He had to leap a branch as high as his brow and stoop under one as low as his knee without slowing, and draw a thorn out of his foot at a run. His kin swore that they would not avenge him if he fell, and he swore four things of his own: to choose a wife for her manners and not her portion, to do no violence to a woman, to refuse no one who asked him for what he had, and to give back before no nine men of another land. The wood came after all of that, and Caílte came after the youth through it.

Cobthach, the Master Ranger at Hibernia's gate, has counted the cords. There are more of them on the old oaks near the gate than anywhere deeper in, and he has written that the Fianna caught most of their candidates in the first hundred strides, while they were still looking back.

Albion calls Murdaigean the goblin wood, for the goblins of the Black Mountains who came into it from the east and dug in along its southern edge; Albion says its wardens drove them there, and Hibernia says Albion sent them. Midgard calls it the wolf wood, and its skalds say the ire wolves and rage wolves of the deep wood are its true lords and everyone else a guest. Spiders have strung the paths between, and corpse crawlers root in the leaf-mould under the webs.

Midgard has its own mark in the wood. In the second summer of the fields a band of five of Midgard's young followed a wounded rage wolf into the deep wood and tracked its blood for half a day. The wolf they found at the end of the trail was not wounded, and it was not alone. The band came back to the Midgard gate four, carrying the fifth between them on a cloak.

Renegades hold Dun Murdaigean, more of them and harder than at the younger fields, under a chieftain who has taken its name.
legend: Murdaigean is the battleground for seasoned bands well along in their seasoning, a dark wood with Dun Murdaigean on a rise in the middle. The renegades are serious here, a lot of Renegade Guardians, each a seasoned band's foe at its strongest, with rangers and commanders, under Renegade Chieftain Murdaigean, a foe for a hardened band of veterans, so bring a full group and siege gear if you want the keep; the three Siege Masters stand at the portal keeps. The wood is full of aggressive spiders, corpse crawlers and wolves, and the goblins along the southern edge, so stay on the paths and do not fight in the trees if you can help it. Raiders call it Murd and say it is the darkest of the four. The goblins are sworn to the Black Mountains Goblins and help each other, and the ire and rage wolves are Angered and do the same, so a fight on the southern edge or in the deep wood brings company.

firstEntry: The light comes down green here and goes out early.

Old knotted cords hang from some of the trees.

loremaster.intro: Murdaigean, the dark wood of the proving fields. Ask me of [Dun Murdaigean], of [the run] the Fianna made there, the [tests] that came before it and the [four oaths], of the knotted [cords], of the [goblins] on its southern edge, the [wolves] of the deep wood and the [wolf sign] Midgard teaches, or of the [webs].

topics.dun murdaigean: The dun on a rise at the heart of the wood, held by renegades: many guardians, with rangers and commanders, under a chieftain who has taken its name, as the renegade chieftains of the fields do.
topics.goblins: Goblins of the Black Mountains who came into the wood from the east in the first summer of the fields and dug in along its southern edge. Albion says its wardens drove them there; Hibernia says Albion sent them. Their watchers cry out at dusk.
topics.wolves: The ire wolves and rage wolves of the deep wood, who hunt in packs and are patient. Midgard calls Murdaigean the wolf wood for them.
topics.webs: The spiders of Murdaigean have strung every path, the large bloated ones near the edges and the death spiders deeper in, and the corpse crawlers root in the leaf-mould under the webs. Some of the webs on the oldest trees are strung over something older.
topics.the run: The last of the Fianna's tests. The youth ran the wood with his hair braided and a tree's length of start, and failed if he was caught, if a braid caught on a branch, or if a dry stick cracked under his foot. Caílte set the pace of the chase. The run ended at the dun. See [cords].
topics.tests: Before the run, a youth of the Fianna had to know the twelve books of poetry and make verse; stand with a shield and a hazel stake while nine spears came at him at once from nine ridges off; keep steady hands; leap a branch at his brow and stoop under one at his knee; and draw a thorn from his foot without slowing. Then he swore the [four oaths].
topics.four oaths: A youth of the Fianna swore to choose a wife for her manners and not her portion, to do no violence to a woman, to refuse no one who asked for what he had, and to give back before no nine men of another land. His kin swore not to avenge him.
topics.cords: Wherever the Fianna caught a runner they knotted a cord to the nearest tree. The oldest oaks of Murdaigean are hung with them, grey with web, thickest near the Hibernian gate: Cobthach, the Master Ranger, says most candidates were caught in the first hundred strides.
topics.wolf sign: Midgard's recruits learn to read wolf sign in Murdaigean before they learn the paths. In the second summer a band of five followed a wounded rage wolf half a day into the deep wood and found an unwounded one waiting with its pack; four came back, carrying the fifth. See [wolves].

book.title: The Green Dark, by Cobthach, Master Ranger at Hibernia's gate in Murdaigean
pages: I was twenty years a ranger of the Path before they gave me the gate at Murdaigean, and I have not looked on a wood I liked less. The light comes down green and thin and goes out an hour before it should. The spiders have strung every path, the corpse crawlers root in the leaf-mould under them, and the wolves keep the deep wood. At night you hear them answer each other across the dark, and the goblins on the southern edge go quiet to listen. On the old oaks by our gate there are cords tied, grey with web and half rotten, and every cord has knots in it.

My grandmother told me what the knots are. When the Fianna ran their young through this wood, they tied a knot on the nearest tree wherever a runner was caught, so that he would know how far he had come. A grown man would come back years after and find his knot, she said, and stand under it a while. He would not say what he thought of there, and nobody asked him. I counted the knots on the one oak by our gate in my first winter here. I stopped at three hundred, because the light had gone, and I have not gone back to finish.

This summer I noticed that the young of our muster braid their hair before they go down into the wood. None of them could tell me who had told them to, and I did not tell them either. Some of them do it badly, with a soldier's thumbs, and the braids come loose on the first branch, and in the morning they sit at the gate with their hair about their faces and say nothing about it. I have only begun walking down with them at dusk as far as the old oak, which is as far as the field will let me, and standing there until the last of them is out of sight among the trees.

The Midgard band's tale reached our gate by way of the Midgard young themselves, who shout it across the wood at ours, as a warning or a boast; I have never been able to tell which. I have set it down as they shout it. Five of their young followed a wounded rage wolf into the deep wood and tracked its blood for half a day, and the wolf at the end of the trail was neither wounded nor alone. They came back four, carrying the fifth on a cloak. I have walked the edge of that deep wood since, as far as I am let, and I have seen the blood trails the wolves leave. They lead inward, always, and they are always fresh. I have told our young to let a bleeding wolf go. Most of them listen. The ones who do not are back at the gate by morning, sitting under the old oak, and they do not want to talk about wolves.

hibernia.story: Hibernia tells Murdaigean as its own, and the oldest proving ground there is: the wood where the Fianna tried their young long before the realms made a field of it. The knotted cords on its oldest trees are the Fianna's marks, and the dun at its heart was the end of their run. Hibernia's young braid their hair before they go down into that wood, and not one of them can say who first told them to.

loremaster.intro: Murdaigean is ours, the oldest proving ground there is, and the proving fields only borrowed it. It was the wood of [the run], where the Fianna tried their young, and the dun at the heart of it, [Dun Murdaigean], was where the run ended. Mind the [webs], and mind what's under them.

topics.the run: When a youth asked to be taken into the Fianna, they braided his hair and gave him a tree's length of start, and then the whole company came after him through Murdaigean. If they caught him, he had failed. If a braid was pulled loose by a branch, or a dry stick cracked under his foot, or the spear shook in his hand, he had failed. He had to leap a branch as high as his brow and go under one as low as his knee, and pull a thorn from his foot without slowing. Nearly all of them failed, and there was no shame in that. The shame was only in not running.

albion.story: Albion tells Murdaigean as the goblin wood. The wardens of the Black Mountains drove a band of goblins out of the passes in the first summer of the fields, and the goblins went west into the wood and dug in along its southern edge. Albion's squires are told that the goblins of Murdaigean are the realm's own unfinished business, and kill them first. Albion has no tale of the wood older than that, and does not dispute the Hibernians' one.

loremaster.intro: Murdaigean is the dark wood of the proving fields, and Albion knows it as the goblin wood. The [goblins] on its southern edge are the realm's own leftovers from the Black Mountains. The Hibernians say the wood was a proving ground of their Fianna before ever it was a field, and Albion has no tale to set against it. The fort at its heart is [Dun Murdaigean].

topics.goblins: In the first summer of the fields the wardens of the Black Mountains drove a band of goblins out of the passes, and the goblins went west into Murdaigean and dug in along its southern edge, where they crawl and watch to this day. Albion's squires are told they are the realm's own unfinished business, and kill them first. The Hibernians say Albion sent them. The wardens' report says only that the goblins went west, and that nobody followed them, and that this was thought at the time to be the end of the matter.

midgard.story: Midgard's skalds call Murdaigean the wolf wood. They hold that the ire wolves and rage wolves of the deep wood are its true lords and that the renegades, the goblins and the realms' young are all guests in it, and Midgard's recruits are taught to read wolf sign before they are taught the paths. The Hibernians' tale of their Fianna the skalds allow, on the ground that it is a good tale and the wolves do not dispute it.

loremaster.intro: Murdaigean. The skalds call it the wolf wood, and they are right: the [wolves] are its lords and the rest are guests. The Hibernians say their Fianna ran their young through it once, and the [goblins] have dug into its southern edge since. The keep in the middle is [Dun Murdaigean]. Learn the wolves' sign before you learn the paths.

topics.wolves: The ire wolves and the rage wolves of Murdaigean hunt the deep wood in packs, and Midgard teaches its young to read their sign before it teaches them the paths. The Hibernians say the wolves are the Fianna's hounds, gone wild when the Fianna left. That may be. A wolf does not care whose it was. It knows the wood, and it knows that the young who come into it are tired, and it is patient.
